justification: The article delivers on its stated differentiator. I fetched the two general comparison pages for this query: Wikipedia's Adjacency_list article derives a theoretical crossover density algebraically (d > 1/64, i.e. ~1.6%) assuming a bit-packed matrix, but reports no measured bytes anywhere; GeeksforGeeks's 'Graph and its Representations' gives Big-O space complexity in five languages but no benchmarked memory and no crossover discussion at all. Neither the two Sedgewick & Wayne pages this article cites nor CLRS's chapter on elementary graph algorithms measure real memory either — all are Big-O only. This article's 'Measuring memory instead of counting Big-O terms' section is a real, runnable GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread measurement (confirmed via run-code.mjs: PASS, 11 blocks / 6 executed) across six edge counts on a disclosed toolchain ('.NET 10.0.12, Windows 11, x64, Core i7-11700K'), placed mid-paragraph rather than as a stamped opening sentence, matching the brief's rule. The measured crossover (roughly 6%-20% of all possible pairs, for C#'s un-packed bool[,] and List<int>) is presented as specific to this runtime and these types, not generalized past what was measured — it explicitly contrasts with, rather than contradicts, Wikipedia's bit-packed theoretical figure, since a bool[,] in .NET is not bit-packed. This is a genuine, checkable differentiator no competing page in this comparison set has. Quote-fabrication check: I independently fetched all three Sedgewick & Wayne quotes and all three Microsoft Learn quotes the article uses. All six match verbatim and are correctly attributed with quotation marks, not passed off as the article's own prose: 'a vertex-indexed array of lists of the vertices connected by an edge to each vertex' (Undirected Graphs page), 'the outdegree of a vertex is the number of edges pointing from it' (Directed Graphs page), 'time proportional to E log E' (Minimum Spanning Trees page, correctly excerpted from a longer sentence), 'implemented as a hash table' (Dictionary<TKey,TValue> docs), and 'using an array whose size is dynamically increased as required' (List<T> docs) all check out exactly. No close paraphrasing found: the article's own explanatory prose around every quote (why Kruskal wants an edge list, why a matrix can't skip an unset cell, why List<T> overhead isn't visible in O(V+E)) is original reasoning, not reworded source material. The worked examples are original constructions (five park junctions A-E; a four-junction one-way trail-connector system with distances) rather than the source textbooks' own running examples (Sedgewick & Wayne's tinyG.txt-style numbered graphs), satisfying the brief's 'do not reuse a source's running example' rule. Sourcing: all 7 front-matter sources resolve to an inline citation at the point their claim is made (the two Sedgewick & Wayne quotes, the CLRS V^2 bound, the MST/Kruskal quote, and the three .NET API pages) — no orphaned or unlinked sources, which is the specific pattern that has capped sibling reviews on this site below 8.5 before. No filler: the opening paragraph states a concrete definition and worked example rather than throat-clearing, there is no boilerplate Introduction/Conclusion/Key-takeaways heading, and the closing 'Choosing a representation' section is a decision guide keyed to the article's own measured crossover, not a restated summary. No placeholder or NEEDS_MARKUS markers found anywhere in the file. No ad code, no ad placeholders. Front matter is accurate and non-clickbait: the title names exactly the three representations covered, and the description ('measure C# memory at each density... a decision guide grounded in real numbers') is a precise, non-inflated summary of what the article actually does. Structure: headings ('The same graph, stored three ways', 'What each operation costs', 'Weighted and directed variants', 'Measuring memory instead of counting Big-O terms', 'When there's no graph to store: implicit graphs', 'Choosing a representation') do not echo any sibling article's heading text in this pillar (checked against all six existing data-structures articles). The one soft observation, not scored as a defect: the article carries only two exercises (a find-the-bug and a predict-the-output), versus four to five in the other data-structures articles reviewed this round; both are well-constructed and correctly withhold their output inside the :::solution block per the pilot-round rule, so this is a depth/pacing note rather than a filler or copying problem.
